Fellowhelpers
FEL-loh-HEL-perz
n. pl. (those who help alongside another; co-workers in a common cause)
A compound of fellow (Old Norse felagi, one who lays down a fee with another, a partner) and helper. The Greek is sunergos, a fellow worker, from sun (with) and ergon (work).

Biblical Definition

John writes to Gaius about the itinerant preachers who had come through, and gives the reason the church must support them: “We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth” (3 John 1:8). A fellowhelper is one who works alongside, and the striking thing in this verse is the object: not fellowhelpers to the preachers, but to the truth. The hospitality Gaius showed was not patronage of men but partnership with a message. He had done it already: “Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers” (3 John 1:5). The doctrine is important because it dignifies the sender as truly as the sent. The man who lodges and funds a preacher is not a spectator to gospel work; he is a fellow worker in it, and he will share its reward. Paul uses the same category of himself toward the Corinthians, refusing any lordship over their faith: “Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand” (2 Corinthians 1:24). Ministry in the New Testament is a fellowship of labour under one Lord, never a clerical caste with an audience.

Modern Corruption

Gospel labour is divided into professionals who do the work and laymen who fund it, so that the supporting believer is treated as a donor rather than a fellow worker with the truth.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors shelter behind this verse. The clerical error treats ordained men as the ministry and the rest of the church as its audience and revenue; the consumer error treats the congregation as customers who purchase religious services and may withhold payment when displeased. Both deny what John says, that the man who receives a preacher becomes a fellowhelper to the truth itself.

The New Testament gives real authority to elders and real honour to the office, and the dictionary holds the two offices of elder and deacon with a plurality of elders as the apostolic pattern. But Paul will not call that authority dominion over faith, and John will not call Gaius a patron. The sender labours with the sent. That is why the household that opens its door, the woman who feeds the itinerant, and the church that funds the missionary are not supporting the work; they are doing it.

Fellow plus helper; Greek sunergos, fellow worker; 3 John 1:8 makes the host a fellowhelper to the truth.
